title: Indirect opposition and connecting rectangles
note:
When the kings do not share a file, rank or diagonal, Silman uses a rectangle to help recognize an indirect opposition relationship. The kings occupy opposite corners, and the other corners complete a rectangle whose corner squares have the same color. His sequence repeatedly changes that rectangle until a direct or diagonal relationship becomes visible.

The method is easiest to learn by pausing after each king move and naming the four corners. A move that preserves the pattern need not make the rectangle smaller immediately. The relevant question is whether the opponent can avoid the later relationship as the kings approach. The diagrams show successive stages of one geometry demonstration, rather than separate endgames to win.

Use the device as a calculation aid, with a stated access goal. Pawns, occupied squares, reserve moves and urgent threats can change which king route matters. The later Part Four example is an explicit warning that taking an indirect opposition can be useless if it prevents the king from getting ahead of its own pawn. Learn the geometry here, then test its purpose in the linked practical reading.

Recognize transitions into direct or diagonal opposition.
An attractive rectangle must serve a practical goal.

ref: A king in front does not solve the rook-pawn exception; PDF 110-112
title: A king in front does not solve the rook-pawn exception
note:
Getting the king ahead of a pawn is a useful starting aim, but the rook-pawn example shows why it cannot be treated as an unconditional winning rule. White has an advanced king and plenty of time to push the h-pawn. Black can nevertheless keep access to the promotion corner and use the edge of the board as a defensive resource.

In the demonstrated line the pawn eventually reaches h7, leaving the black king on h8 without a legal move and without being in check. That is stalemate. If the defender voluntarily leaves the corner at the wrong moment, the outcome changes; the lesson is the availability of a drawing defense, not that every move in the position draws.

Compare this with the existing introductory rook-pawn reading before applying the following non-rook-pawn rules. State the actual king squares and inspect legal moves at the end of the variation. Do not stop calculating just because promotion is one step away. A useful practice explanation should identify the corner the defender needs, the pawn push that ends the game, and why the advanced attacking king cannot manufacture an escape square beyond the board.
keyIdeas: Check the pawn file before using king-placement rules.
Corner access can outweigh the attacking king’s advance.
Verify stalemate with legal moves.

title: King one square ahead: compare both sides to move
note:
With the king immediately ahead of a non-rook-pawn, the side to move can determine whether the defender must give way. Silman presents one starting arrangement twice in effect: with White to move, Black can keep the barrier; with Black to move, White can use the conceded side to make progress. The pieces alone do not specify the problem.

The winning technique alternates king access with timely pawn support. When the defender retreats, the attacking king should consider advancing instead of automatically seeking another opposition. When the defender approaches the pawn, a pawn move can secure the progress already made. Walking away from the pawn in pursuit of a king maneuver can simply lose it.

Reconstruct the starting position with White’s king on d3, pawn on d2 and Black’s king on d5. Play it from each side with each turn assignment, explaining every change of plan. The verified branches illustrate the method and the starting win/draw contrast; they are not a demand to reproduce a single forced script. This elementary case should be learned before generalizing to other ranks, the sixth-rank exception or positions with additional pawns.

Take safe king access when it is offered.
Keep the pawn protected while the king advances.

title: King two squares ahead and a reserve pawn move
note:
The distance between king and pawn can provide a useful extra move. In Silman’s example the white king is on d4, the pawn remains on d2 and the black king is on d6. If Black must move, the familiar access technique is available. If White must move, advancing the pawn only to d3 passes the decision to Black while preserving the king arrangement.

The important resource is the unused pawn move. Advancing a pawn changes the position permanently; spending two squares at once can discard a tempo that would be useful later. The example explains why a king farther ahead can be more effective than a king directly in front, even though the board initially looks similar.

Compare the same board with White and Black to move, then compare it with the previous one-square case. Describe exactly what the pawn move changes and why the resulting position is familiar. Keep the scope of the rule clear: this is king and a non-rook-pawn against a lone king in the reviewed arrangement. The rook-pawn corner exception and the safety of the pawn still need separate attention in actual play.

Silman begins this practical test with an apparent contradiction: White can take an indirect opposition and still lose the chance to win. The reason is that the chosen route fails to get the king ahead of its pawn. Recognizing the geometry correctly is not enough when it serves the wrong destination.

With White’s king on f1, pawn on d4 and Black’s king on h8, White should consider the route through e2, d3 and c4. It advances toward the pawn while avoiding an early confrontation with the enemy king on the kingside. The source’s contrasting f2 route allows Black to establish the familiar drawing barrier. title: Retreat squares and the sixth-rank king
note:
The defender’s available retreat squares explain why similar-looking pawn endings have different results. In the first comparison, Black can retreat straight back as the pawn advances and use a final stalemate. In the next case, correct king placement restores the same defensive pattern. Looking only at who appears to have opposition misses the reason the defense works.

When White’s king has reached the sixth rank ahead of a non-rook-pawn, the defender can run out of the retreat needed to maintain that barrier. Silman contrasts this with the earlier positions so the student can see what changed on the board. The winning method depends on controlling the pawn’s path and the remaining escape squares, rather than invoking a slogan about opposition.

The final example requires an accurate approach to an advanced pawn. One king route keeps the win; a tempting alternative lets the defender rebuild the drawing position. Practice the comparison by naming the defender’s intended retreat after each pawn push. Count legal moves at the alleged stalemate, and retain the rook-pawn exception when moving these patterns to the edge.

A sixth-rank king changes the available defensive space.

title: Preserve the right opposition during the approach
note:
A correct opposition relationship at the start is not a license to respond mechanically for the rest of the ending. Silman compares the kings on e1 and e8 with a white pawn on e2, first with White to move and then with Black to move. The change of turn alters the result, but the defender still has to navigate the transition accurately.

In the defensive branch, a later position places White’s king on d2 and Black’s on e6. Black needs to preserve the relationship that blocks the approaching king. The source’s d6 move maintains the drawing route; several neighboring king moves allow White to obtain a useful opposition and advance. The practice comparison checks selected alternatives rather than assuming all sensible-looking moves are equivalent.

Use the starting position to predict the outcome, then pause again at the intermediate decision. Explain why the next move contributes to the same defensive aim. The exercise should test understanding of transitions, not only recognition of a diagram. An available pawn move also belongs in the calculation, because it can transfer the move without changing the placement of the kings.

title: Mutual zugzwang and the trebuchet
note:
A trebuchet is a mutual zugzwang: each king is tied to protecting its pawn, and the side forced to move loses that protection. Silman’s compact example has White’s king on g5 and pawn on f4 against Black’s king on e4 and pawn on f5. Either turn assignment loses for the player who must move.

That result makes timing essential when more pawns are present. In the following example, both kings collect peripheral pawns and approach the central contact. Rushing directly to the apparently natural square can give the opponent the favorable version of the same mutual dependency. The successful route arranges for the other player to make the unwanted king move.

For study, first learn the four-piece mechanism without the distraction of the outer pawns. Then return to the longer example and identify the move that determines who will be tied down. A pawn capture can gain material while giving away the critical tempo. Calculate through the resulting king-and-pawn ending; do not stop at the capture or assume that an active-looking king move must improve the position.
keyIdeas: Mutual zugzwang makes the move a liability.
Time the approach so the opponent must yield.
Evaluate a capture through the resulting ending.

title: Choose the pawn ending left after the capture
note:
When a pawn cannot be saved, the defender may still choose a king square that makes the remaining single-pawn ending drawable. Silman’s first example shows Black abandoning a pawn while arranging to meet White’s recapture with the right opposition. A neighboring retreat loses because it leaves a different king relationship after the same capture.

The comparison one rank farther up the board demonstrates the limit of that resource. The attacking king is sufficiently advanced that the defender cannot reproduce the earlier barrier. A third example places the pawn ahead of its king and restores a drawing pattern. These are decisions about the position after liquidation, not a general instruction to surrender pawns or exchange whenever behind.

Before making the capture, place the remaining pawn and both kings mentally on their final squares and state whose turn follows. Compare that position with a verified single-pawn pattern. In practice, replay the drawing branches to their stalemate finish and the winning branch to a secure promotion route. This joins the earlier study of favorable exchanges to a concrete endgame test: the value of the trade depends on what remains.

title: Doubled pawns as reserve moves
note:
Doubled pawns are not automatically a liability in a simplified ending. In Silman’s examples, the rear pawn can supply a waiting move that the leading pawn and king need. Its usefulness depends on survival, timing and the resulting legal moves, rather than the visual appearance of two pawns on one file.

The first position changes outcome with the turn. White can bring the king forward to protect the advanced pawn; if Black moves first, that pawn can be attacked before the same arrangement is secured. In the winning version, the rear pawn is preserved until its move transfers the opposition at the decisive moment.

The second example adds a promotion sacrifice. Allowing the defender to capture the new queen can leave a familiar winning king-and-pawn ending with the remaining pawn. A natural-looking king move instead produces stalemate. Practice both continuations and count the defender’s legal moves before choosing. These are specific non-rook-pawn endings; they do not establish a verdict on doubled pawns in the middlegame, nor do extra rook-pawns necessarily cure the board-edge stalemate problem.

title: Rook-pawn endings can stalemate the stronger side
note:
The defending king does not always have to occupy the promotion corner. Silman shows a second drawing mechanism: the attacking king can be trapped on the rook-pawn’s file while the defender controls its exit. When the pawn can no longer move, the player with the extra pawn may be the one stalemated.

The contrast between an attacking king on g7 and one on h7 makes the escape route visible. In the h7 example, Black to move can establish the barrier; with White to move, the king can escape to g7 and preserve a win. Adding more h-pawns only provides additional waiting moves if the same trap survives. The source follows three rook-pawns until White has no legal move.

For practice, identify whose king lacks an exit and whose turn it will be when the pawn moves run out. The final marked-square diagram is a schematic, not a fully specified legal position; do not invent kings and call it an additional puzzle. Apply the lesson to exchanges by asking whether the attacking king can leave the edge before the defender closes the route.
keyIdeas: Check whether the attacking king can leave the edge.
Extra rook-pawns may only delay stalemate.
State which player is stalemated.

title: The square rule and the move that changes the race
note:
The square rule gives a quick first answer to a simple race between an unescorted pawn and a king. Build a square from the pawn to its promotion rank, extending toward the pursuing king. If the king can enter that square in time, it can catch the pawn in the unobstructed case shown by Silman. If it cannot, the pawn can promote before the chase succeeds.

The source compares a white a-pawn on a4 with the black king on f7. With Black to move, the king can enter the square; with White to move, a5 shrinks the square before Black can enter. The separate a5 diagram makes the change visible. Whose turn it is therefore belongs in the shortcut, just as it does in opposition.

Use the square to predict the result, then confirm it by counting legal pawn pushes and king steps. The supplied position has no obstruction or supporting white king near the race. Other pieces, controlled squares or a different pawn move option require a fresh calculation. This section is the foundation for later pawn races; the book’s outside-passers and diversion examples remain for future reading.
keyIdeas: Draw the square to the promotion rank.
Account for the move before deciding whether the king can enter.
Verify that the route is legal and unobstructed.

title: Recognize Lucena and cut off the defending king
note:
Lucena provides a concrete target for converting an extra non-rook-pawn in a rook ending. The pawn has reached the seventh rank and its king occupies the promotion square. The defender’s rook prevents a convenient exit while the defending king remains close enough to restrict the other side. The attacker must coordinate king and rook to clear the pawn’s path safely.

In Silman’s example, the first useful operation is a rook check that pushes the defending king farther away and keeps it cut off. Repeated checks on the neighboring file do not produce the same improvement. Count the access gained by the check rather than treating any forcing move as progress.

Study the position as an arrangement of jobs: the pawn needs a free promotion square, the king needs shelter after leaving it, and the rook must limit the enemy king while preparing that shelter. The checked starting position is won, but a win still needs a procedure. This is a specific non-rook-pawn pattern; it does not imply that every rook and seventh-rank pawn ending is automatically won, or that the defender’s rook placement can be ignored.
keyIdeas: Identify the pawn, king exit and checking barrier.
Drive the defending king away while keeping it cut off.
Judge checks by the access they create.

title: Lucena: distinguish a detour from losing the win
note:
After the defending king has been pushed aside, it is tempting to move the attacking king immediately. Silman follows those attempts to show why a bare escape is insufficient. Checks can send the king back, or drive it away from the pawn until the defending rook attacks that pawn and forces the king to return.

The source describes these choices as wrong for its teaching plan. Exact tablebase checks of the supplied position show an important distinction: the candidate king moves and the extra rook check still retain a theoretical win. Their illustrated continuations fail to demonstrate progress; they are not immediate drawing blunders. A student should understand how to improve the plan without being told the result has changed when it has not.

By contrast, moving the king far enough to abandon protection allows the rook to capture the pawn and draw in the explicit branch. Compare the positions after the checks and identify whether the pawn remains safe. The central question is not simply whether the king escapes, but whether it can remain usefully near the pawn with an answer to the next check. This prepares the purpose of the bridge-building rook move.
keyIdeas: Escaping checks must preserve pawn support.
A non-progress detour can still retain a theoretical win.
Losing the pawn is a different kind of error.

title: Build the bridge before exposing the king
note:
The bridge is a rook placement that will later block checks while the king remains close enough to protect it. In Silman’s example, the rook prepares on the fourth rank before the king leaves the promotion square. The move’s value becomes clear only after the defender begins checking the exposed king.

The king then approaches the prepared rook through squares that keep the pawn protected. Once it reaches the appropriate square, the rook steps onto the checking file and interposes. The king protects that rook, so simply capturing the bridge does not solve the defender’s problem. This converts the rook from a tool that cuts off the enemy king into a shelter for its own king.

Practice the procedure in stages: cutoff, preparation, supported king route and interposition. At each check, name the pawn’s defender before moving. The source’s premature king step lets the checking rook take the pawn and draw; the correct route preserves the winning material and reaches the bridge. The reviewed line is a model against the shown defense, not a claim that every legal defending move follows the same script. Philidor and other defensive positions are separate future readings.
keyIdeas: Prepare the rook before the king leaves shelter.
Keep the pawn defended at each check.
Block with a rook protected by the king.

title: Recognize the Philidor defensive goal
note:
A pawn advantage, an advanced king and an active-looking rook do not by themselves establish a winning rook ending. Silman introduces Philidor with a position in which the defender still has the resources to prevent the attacker from coordinating king and pawn. The task is to recognize that defensive arrangement and preserve it.

In the supplied example, the defending king stands in front of the pawn while the attacking king has not crossed the rank the rook can guard. The defender needs a plan for restricting king access and a clear trigger for changing the rook’s job. That combination is what makes the draw practical to execute.

Compare this starting position with the earlier Lucena reading. Name the pawn rank, the attacking king’s access and the defending king’s relationship to the pawn. Treat the comparison as recognition practice before memorizing moves. The detailed method follows in Pure Philidor; the intervening passive-rook examples explain what the defender should avoid and why the pawn file can change the result.

title: Punish a passive rook with a transfer
note:
A rook confined to defending the back rank can leave the opposing king free to support a decisive attack. Silman’s first example places the pawn on d6 and the attacking king beside it. The attacker can transfer the rook to the other side of the board, creating a back-rank check that the defender cannot answer satisfactorily.

The c-pawn example uses the same idea with a concrete change of move order. The rook transfer forces the king to respond, a pawn check displaces it again, and the next rook check wins the defending rook. The lesson is to coordinate king, pawn and rook threats rather than repeat checks from an ineffective file.

For practice, identify what ties the defending rook to its rank and what the transfer threatens. Then follow the source’s c-pawn line to the actual material gain. The d-pawn passage supplies a first move and threat rather than a complete forced line; do not invent a silent opponent reply. These positions illustrate the cost of this particular passive arrangement. The next reading tests the board-edge exception, so inactivity alone should not be used as a universal verdict.
keyIdeas: Identify the threat that ties the defender’s rook down.
Transfer to a file that creates a decisive check.
Coordinate the pawn check with the rook transfer.

note:

The demonstrated checks return the kings and rooks to a position where White has made no progress. Pushing the pawn impatiently then allows a checking tactic that turns the tables. The example should train the student to distinguish a draw that requires accurate play from permission to make arbitrary moves. The source also identifies rook-pawns as exceptions in these passive defensive arrangements.

Keep the scope precise: a knight-pawn here means a b- or g-pawn, not a pawn accompanied by a knight. Do not generalize the result to every ending containing an edge pawn, or confuse it with the earlier king-and-rook-pawn stalemate lesson.

title: Philidor: hold the rank before checking
note:
The basic Philidor method begins by denying the attacking king entry to the rank in front of its pawn. In the supplied position, Black plays Rh6 and keeps the rook guarding White’s sixth rank, which is Black’s third rank. This is why the same method is called third-rank defense. White cannot bring the king forward while that barrier is intact.

The defender can wait with the rook while retaining the king in front of the pawn. Checking from behind too soon gives the attacker a chance to advance the king and use the pawn as shelter. The resulting diagram 135 is still a theoretical draw, as the source explicitly acknowledges, but its advanced defensive method is outside this passage. The two natural checking attempts shown there lose.

There is also a qualification to the source’s warning about Rf7 followed by Ra8: exact checks retain a draw, with resources such as a later Rf1. Treat that as a less direct route, not an immediate losing blunder. For this lesson, learn the straightforward rank barrier and explain the future trigger for abandoning it. The goal is a reliable defensive procedure with correctly stated outcomes.
keyIdeas: Guard White’s sixth rank, Black’s third rank.
Wait while the pawn still offers shelter to the king.
Distinguish harder defense from a lost position.

ref: Switch to rear checks when the pawn advances; PDF 221-222
title: Switch to rear checks when the pawn advances
note:
The pawn advance changes the defensive task. Once White pushes to e6 in the source example, the defending rook moves away from the guarded rank and prepares long-range checks from behind. The attacker has used the pawn move that previously could have sheltered the king, so the rook can now disrupt attempts to bring that king forward.

This is a timed change of method. Continuing to wait on the old rank would ignore the newly available king entry, while leaving too early would allow the attacking king to retain pawn cover. Ask what changed on the board before deciding whether the rook should restrict or check. The pawn’s rank and the king’s available shelter explain the switch.

The source also examines blocking a check with the attacking rook. A rook exchange then leads to a familiar drawn king-and-pawn ending, ending in stalemate in the displayed line. That connects this defense to the previous pawn-ending package: a trade is safe because of the precise position left behind. Practice the complete sequence, then repeat from the moment of the pawn push so the trigger becomes recognizable without replaying the whole lesson from memory.
keyIdeas: The pawn push is the trigger for switching methods.
Check from a distance when the king lacks pawn shelter.
Verify the pawn ending before exchanging rooks.

title: Cut off the defending king to preserve the win
note:
Keeping the opposing king away from the pawn can be more effective than giving another check. In Silman’s winning example the extra pawn is not yet close to promotion, but the defending king is too far away to help. The attacker’s rook can establish a file barrier that prevents it from reaching the front of the pawn and creating a Philidor defense.

The move Rf1 gives the rook a continuing job: exclude the king while White’s king and pawn make progress. If Black contests the file by offering a rook exchange, the resulting pawn ending is won for White. The source’s short exchange line illustrates why the defender cannot simply remove the barrier without considering what remains.

Compare this with Lucena’s earlier king cutoff. The pawn is less advanced here, but the purpose is the same: deny the defending king a useful route to the decisive area. Before transferring the rook, identify the file that must stay controlled and check whether a rook trade helps or hurts. The passage gives a conversion plan and a selected exchange comparison; it is not a complete forced promotion sequence against every legal defense.
keyIdeas: Deny the defending king a route in front of the pawn.
Use a file barrier to support king-and-pawn progress.
Check the pawn ending if the defender offers a rook trade.

title: Cut off the attacking king to save the position
note:
A king cutoff can also defend a weakness. In Silman’s final example, White wants to bring the king toward the d5-pawn and combine its attack with the rook. If White moves first, the source demonstrates that route and the capture of the pawn. With Black to move, the rook can occupy the c-file and prevent the king from joining the attack.

The rook then creates pressure against White’s f-pawn while preserving the file barrier. Activity and restriction work together: the defender is not merely checking whenever possible, nor passively protecting d5. The useful rook move changes the attacking king’s access and gives the opponent another problem to address.

Practice both turn assignments, naming the king entry square before selecting a rook move. In the defensive line, explain why the rook returns along the c-file rather than abandoning its main responsibility. This is a nine-piece practical ending, so its source win/draw judgments are supported here by legal replay and finite-depth engine checks, not by the exact tablebase evidence used for the smaller examples. The lesson is the demonstrated mechanism and its conditions, not a universal rule that cutting off a king always draws.
keyIdeas: Identify the king route that makes the pawn vulnerable.
Combine a file barrier with pressure on another pawn.
Keep the rook’s main defensive responsibility in view.
